Denver.metaTitle: Denver, CO Sewer Lateral Lining & CIPP Rules
Denver.metaDescription: Denver's DOTI publishes strict trenchless sewer repair rules, from Hold Harmless Letters to camera inspections. See who owns your lateral and where CIPP lining fits.
Denver.article:
Denver's Own Trenchless Rulebook Sets the Bar for Sewer Repairs

Denver's Department of Transportation & Infrastructure doesn't leave trenchless sewer repair to a contractor's judgment call. A 2024 DOTI document, "Requirements for PW Repairs and SUDP Work," spells out when pipe bursting is allowed beneath a sidewalk or curb and what a crew must prove before, during, and after: three days' notice, real site photographs, and a signed Hold Harmless Letter. The city also lists what does and does not justify going trenchless — age of the structure, hardscaping, buried utilities, and mature landscaping count; skipping a mess in the yard does not. As the rulebook puts it, "Simply avoiding yard disruption is not a valid reason." Denver's scrutiny reflects a long institutional memory: the Wastewater Management Division says it has provided sewer service for more than 150 years.

Who Owns the Building Sewer Under Denver Code

Denver's code, Chapter 56 of the Denver Revised Municipal Code, calls the pipe running from a house to the street a "building sewer," defined with unusual precision: it begins five feet outside the exterior wall and runs to and includes the tap where it meets the public main. In many cities the tap belongs to the utility; in Denver, it belongs to the homeowner. The code puts maintenance squarely on the property owner, and city rules add that this duty holds whether the pipe sits on public or private ground. Even the stretch of building sewer running through the right-of-way stays private property under Denver's title rules. If a backup traces to the city's side of the tap, a crew responds; on the owner's side, the city notifies them and steps back.

Permits, Licensing, and Inspection for Lateral Work in Denver

Nobody may open a sewer line in Denver without a DOTI permit kept on site and ready to show any officer who asks. The work must be done by a state-licensed plumber or a certified drainlayer, and a business laying sewers in Denver separately needs a city license backed by a bond — a figure carried forward from the 1950s at $1,000. A contractor must give at least 24 hours' notice before tying into the public sewer, excluding Sundays and holidays, with an inspector present at the connection; work done without notice is treated as defective and can be redone at the contractor's expense. A repair permit typically runs $55 per inspection trip, and a cutoff at the main is required whenever excavation comes within 10 feet of the property line.

What the City Won't Let Flow Into the System

Denver's code bars stormwater, roof drainage, and groundwater from the sanitary sewer outright, except in the few areas still running on older combined lines — a legacy the code acknowledges while making clear new combined sewers are no longer permitted. Sump pump discharge and anything solid or thick enough to clog a pipe are also prohibited. City guidance points to grease, wipes, and diapers as common backup culprits, along with tree roots, drawn to the moisture inside sewer pipe and able to work into even a pinhole crack. An owner within 300 feet of a public sewer and 1,000 feet of the main can be ordered to connect within 90 days of notice.

Where Lining Fits Under Denver's Repair Rules

Denver's 2024 trenchless rules focus on pipe bursting, but the same logic — permit first, document everything, prove the pipe works before backfilling — applies to any trenchless method on a building sewer. A cured-in-place liner is typically installed through an existing cleanout, avoiding the wide, cleared trench the code otherwise expects at a connection to the public main. Because it reinforces a pipe from the inside rather than replacing it in an open cut, lining can address cracked, corroded, or root-intruded clay and cast iron without disturbing the ten-foot separation Denver requires between sewer and water lines. The inspection standard applies regardless of method: a post-repair camera must run from the main to the cleanout with water flowing, and a line that can't move water cleanly is a failed repair.

When a Liner Won't Solve the Problem

A liner cures against the inside of the existing pipe wall, so it takes on the exact path — and the exact defects — of whatever is already there. Denver's guidance draws a hard line: minor belly issues are not accepted, and standing water in the line at inspection means immediate denial, since a pipe that can't drain isn't considered functional. A section settled out of grade has lost the fall needed to carry waste to the main, and no liner can restore that slope; the sagging run has to be excavated and reset. The same goes for a pipe crushed or squeezed out of round by soil or roots — lining can seal cracks, but it can't force a collapsed section back into a circle or turn an undersized line into a larger one. Denver's rule that a failed post-repair video means immediate excavation shows how firmly the city treats these limits.

A City Built on Clay Pipe: Denver's Housing Age and Sewer History

Denver's housing stock spans a mining-camp founding in 1858, a railroad boom, a silver-price crash, and a modern building surge. Census data puts 17.2% of the city's roughly 352,600 housing units up before 1940 and 35.5% before 1960, with another 28.1% built between 1940 and 1969 — meaning well over half of Denver's homes were plumbed before PVC pipe or trenchless repair existed. Those decades generally paired with clay and cast-iron building sewers, materials the city's rules still address directly, including a provision letting a sewer more than ten years old keep serving a new building only if the city tests it and finds it still meets code. With 28.7% of Denver's housing built since 2000, the older half of the city is where a camera inspection of the lateral usually comes first, to see whether a section can be relined or must come out of the ground.
faq: Who is responsible for the building sewer between my house and the street in Denver?

Under Denver Revised Municipal Code Chapter 56, the building sewer is privately owned and maintained by the property owner, and the code defines that pipe as extending all the way to and including the tap where it joins the public sewer main.
Does Denver require a permit for sewer lateral repair, including trenchless methods?

Yes. Denver Municipal Code Section 56-103 requires a written permit from DOTI before any building or private sewer is opened, altered, or repaired, and the work must be performed by a state-licensed plumber or a city-certified drainlayer.
What does Denver require before approving a trenchless pipe repair?

DOTI's 2024 trenchless requirements call for at least three days' notice, site photographs, and a signed Hold Harmless Letter, and state that a valid reason for going trenchless includes things like old structures or hardscaping, but not simply avoiding yard disruption.
Can a cured-in-place liner fix a bellied or sagging sewer lateral in Denver?

No. Denver's own trenchless guidance states that minor belly issues will not be accepted, because a liner takes the shape of the existing pipe and cannot restore the slope a sagging section has lost; that section has to be excavated and reset.
How old is Denver's sewer system, and does that affect lateral repairs?

The Wastewater Management Division has provided sewer service for more than 150 years, and Census data shows 35.5% of Denver housing predates 1960, meaning many laterals are original clay or cast iron pipe that a contractor should camera-inspect before choosing a repair method.

Aurora.metaTitle: Aurora, CO Sewer Lateral Repair & Lining Rules
Aurora.metaDescription: Aurora Water can suspend water service over a failed sewer lateral. Learn who owns the line, permit rules, and where CIPP lining fits Aurora city code for homeowners.
Aurora.article:
Aurora's Unusual Enforcement Tool: Water Shutoff Over a Bad Sewer Lateral

Aurora Water runs both the water system and the wastewater collection system for the city, and that combined authority gives it a tool most cities don't have: the power to shut off a home's water service to force a sewer problem to get fixed. Under the city's code, Aurora Water's general manager may suspend water service to reduce or eliminate wastewater flow when a service line's condition threatens the sewer system, property, the environment, or health and safety. As the code puts it, the general manager may act "when the general manager finds that the use of the service line or other building sewer components in their present condition endanger the public sewer system, public or private property, the environment, or the health or safety of occupants or the public." That leverage exists because Aurora Water bills for both utilities on one account and also collects a connection charge for the Metro Wastewater Reclamation District, now Metro Water Recovery, as that district's agent. Ignoring a failing lateral here risks more than a backup.

Who Owns the Service Line in Aurora

Aurora's code puts ownership of the service line on the property owner and draws the boundary further out than some cities do. The owner is responsible for maintenance and repair "from the building served to the tap connection, including any tapping saddle on the public sewer main" — even the fitting where the lateral joins the city's pipe belongs to the homeowner. The general manager also decides when a line has failed: if a section no longer carries waste to the main, or lets groundwater seep in or wastewater leak out, the owner must repair or replace it at their own cost. The city reserves a narrow right to fix a line itself, at city expense, only in the right-of-way and only when it serves the broader system; otherwise the decision and the bill are the owner's.

Getting a Permit and Passing Inspection

Nobody may open, connect to, or disturb a public sewer in Aurora without a written permit, issued along one of two tracks: residential and commercial, or industrial waste. Building-sewer applications go through the building division, while work in the public right-of-way needs a separate public improvement permit, and contractors must meet the licensing, permitting, and bonding rules set elsewhere in city code. A new or reused building sewer qualifies only if the general manager examines and tests it and finds it meets every article requirement, new pipe or old. Once work is done, the applicant must notify public works so the connection is made under an Aurora Water representative's supervision, and open excavations must stay barricaded and lit.

Keeping Stormwater and Grease Out of the System

Aurora's code is direct about what cannot enter a sanitary sewer: roof downspouts, foundation drains, areaway drains, and sump pumps may not tie into a building sewer feeding the public system, and stormwater, surface water, and groundwater are barred outright. Grease gets its own rule — wastewater carrying enough grease or oil to solidify or turn viscous at normal temperatures is not allowed, and a property generating it must install and maintain its own prevention equipment. The mandatory-connection rule works much like it does regionally: once a public sewer sits within a set distance, the owner can be required to connect within a set window after notice, ending reliance on a septic system.

Where Trenchless Repair Fits

Aurora's code doesn't devote a chapter specifically to trenchless methods the way Denver's does, but nothing in the wastewater article singles out lining or pipe bursting as prohibited, and the general permit and inspection framework covers any method a licensed contractor uses. A cured-in-place liner installed through a cleanout avoids the open trench the code otherwise contemplates for new construction, while still meeting the requirement that any connection be gastight and watertight, with deviations from standard materials approved by the general manager beforehand. Because Aurora treats a leaking or infiltrating lateral as grounds for enforcement under the water-suspension rule, relining before it reaches that point is often the more practical route for a homeowner who wants both utilities to keep running.

What a Liner Can't Fix

A liner only works as well as the pipe shape it fills, and Aurora's enforcement rules exist because a degraded line eventually stops carrying flow the way code demands. A section that has settled and lost slope cannot be brought back to grade from the inside; the sag has to be excavated and rebuilt so the pipe falls correctly toward the main. The same holds for a lateral crushed or squeezed out of round by shifting soil: lining can seal a crack or smooth corrosion, but it cannot push a collapsed pipe back into round, or turn a smaller line into a larger one. Since Aurora's general manager can force a fix once a line endangers the system, a homeowner is better off knowing upfront whether lining or excavation is the right answer.

Aurora's Growth Boom and What It Means for Aging Laterals

Aurora's history explains a lot about what is likely running under its streets. The city began in 1890 as the town of Fletcher, incorporated in 1903, and didn't take its present shape until military and aviation installations — Fitzsimons Army Hospital, Lowry Air Force Base, and Buckley Field — drove housing construction outward from Denver's edge. Census figures show just 0.9% of Aurora's roughly 150,200 housing units predate 1940 and only 7.7% predate 1960; the real growth shows in the 13% built between 1940 and 1969 and the 28% built since 2000, reflecting Aurora's run as one of the fastest-growing cities in the country in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Most laterals here are therefore mid-century or newer, but a boom era also means a large share of pipe reaching the same age at once, exactly what Aurora Water's enforcement authority was built to manage.
faq: Can Aurora really shut off my water because of a sewer lateral problem?

Yes. Aurora City Code Section 138-262(m)(4) authorizes the general manager to suspend water service to a building when the condition of the service line endangers the public sewer system, property, the environment, or public health and safety.
Who owns the sewer service line in Aurora?

The property owner retains ownership and is responsible for maintenance and repair of the service line from the building to the tap connection, including the tapping saddle on the public sewer main, under Aurora City Code Section 138-262(m)(1).
Do I need a permit to repair a sewer lateral in Aurora?

Yes. Aurora City Code Section 138-262(a) makes it unlawful to uncover, connect to, or disturb a public sewer without a written permit, and contractors must meet the city's licensing and bonding requirements.
Can a sewer liner fix a lateral that has lost its slope in Aurora?

No. A cured-in-place liner takes the shape of the existing pipe, so a section that has settled and lost grade still needs to be excavated and rebuilt; lining cannot restore the fall needed to carry wastewater to the main.
Why does Aurora's sewer system involve two treatment providers?

Aurora operates its own 5-million-gallon-per-day Sand Creek Water Reclamation Facility for reuse water, while sending the rest of its wastewater to Metro Water Recovery's regional treatment plant as a member district.

Lakewood.metaTitle: Lakewood, CO Sewer Lateral Rules by District
Lakewood.metaDescription: Lakewood has no citywide sewer utility - over 20 special districts each set their own lateral rules. Find your district and see where CIPP lining and pipe bursting fit.
Lakewood.article:
Lakewood Has No Single Sewer Utility — And That Changes Everything

Most cities have one sewer department a homeowner can call. Lakewood doesn't. The city's own Public Works Department serves only about 8,000 customers in north Lakewood, while the rest of the roughly 156,000 residents get sewer service from one of more than twenty special sanitation districts — Bancroft-Clover, Northwest Lakewood, Green Mountain, Bear Creek, Alameda, and more, each with its own board, rate schedule, and repair rules. The city's map of sewer district boundaries lays out 23 service areas, including one carved out just for the Denver Federal Center. A homeowner calling the wrong number gets nowhere; the city points residents to its "My Neighborhood" lookup tool, or a printed provider list and district map, just to find which agency to call.

Finding Out Who Actually Owns Your Lateral

Once a homeowner identifies their district, the ownership rule looks similar agency to agency, though wording differs enough to matter. In north Lakewood, the city states that responsibility for the property lateral, extending all the way to the main, lies with the owner. Bancroft-Clover frames it as everything from the point of connection on the district's main to the building, and says outright it isn't responsible for damage caused by a customer's line or interior plumbing. Northwest Lakewood Sanitation District is even more specific, holding the homeowner responsible for the actual tap connection and noting the district only takes over at that point, usually under the street. Green Mountain's wording is shorter but reaches the same conclusion: ownership runs to the main.

Permits and Inspections Depend on Your District

Because Lakewood has no single sewer authority, permitting for lateral work depends on which agency serves the address. The city requires a Certificate of Sewer Service Availability, signed by whichever provider covers the property, before it will issue a building permit. Within north Lakewood, the city's rules call for PVC sewer pipe meeting ASTM D3034, elastomeric gasket joints, and a minimum SDR of 35, installed to proper line and grade in dedicated streets. Bancroft-Clover runs a separate contractor approval process: a $5,000 surety bond, proof of insurance, a $25 annual license fee, and an inspector's sign-off on tap, pipe, and bedding with 24 hours' notice before backfilling, using Schedule 40 or SDR 35 pipe and grade minimums of 2% for four-inch line and 1% for six-inch — none of which carries to a different district next door.

Backups, Grease, and the City's Reimbursement Limits

Grease and stormwater rules follow the same patchwork pattern. The city's rules for its own area prohibit foreign water — stormwater, surface water, groundwater, roof runoff — from entering the sanitary system, and require grease interceptors at food-service properties, capping grease and oil content at 100 milligrams per liter. Northwest Lakewood's district reports most backups trace to grease and root intrusion together, which is why it cleans roughly a third of its pipe network every year and cameras the whole system on a six-year rotation. For north Lakewood customers, a backup from a blockage in a city-owned main can qualify for reimbursement, capped at $5,000 per claim and filed within 90 days, and it won't cover costs already payable under insurance. Elsewhere, a district's own claims process, where one exists, applies instead.

Where Trenchless Repair Is Allowed — And Where It Needs a Waiver

Trenchless repair shows up explicitly in only one Lakewood-area rulebook reviewed here, with a condition attached. As the district itself puts it, "Bancroft-Clover only allows pipe bursting with a signed waiver from the property owner," because inspectors cannot visually verify a burst-and-replaced pipe the way they can one laid in an open trench. A cured-in-place liner works differently: installed through an existing cleanout, it leaves the original pipe wall in place with a new liner cured against it, a repair a camera pass can verify directly. Because Lakewood's districts haven't all published lining-specific rules, a homeowner's best move is the one the city recommends for everything: confirm which agency has jurisdiction, then ask that inspector what it wants before approving trenchless work.

When Lining Isn't the Right Tool

Lining only reinforces the pipe already there, so it inherits the same shape and slope, for better or worse. A lateral settled into a low spot no longer carries the grade district specifications require, whether that's Bancroft-Clover's 1% to 2% minimum or the city's line-and-grade standard, and a liner cured inside a sagging pipe still lets water pool at the low point; the fix is to excavate and reset that section, not line over it. A pipe gone oval under soil pressure, or crushed by roots through an old joint, presents the same limit: lining seals a crack but cannot force the pipe back into round, or turn a line into a larger size. For a district like Northwest Lakewood, where much of the network is mid-century clay, sorting a fixable crack from real collapse first saves a homeowner from paying for a liner that won't hold.

A City Incorporated Late, Built Early: Lakewood's Housing Age

Lakewood did not become a city until June 24, 1969, incorporating as Jefferson City before quickly taking the Lakewood name, with a population already over 90,000 — meaning the housing and pipe came generations before the government that now oversees only a sliver of the sewer system. Local sanitation districts organized even earlier: Green Mountain Park in 1951, Bancroft-Clover in the early 1950s, and Northwest Lakewood in 1954, each serving development that predated any citywide utility. Census figures back this up: 16.6% of Lakewood's roughly 73,000 housing units predate 1960, and another 32.7% went up between 1940 and 1969, meaning close to half the city's homes date to the district era, often on vitrified clay pipe Northwest Lakewood's own materials call standard for the mid-1950s with a 60-to-75-year life. With only 16.8% built since 2000, many laterals here are old enough that a homeowner's first call should be to find which sewer district owns the ground under their yard.
faq: Does the City of Lakewood run the sewer system for the whole city?

No. The City of Lakewood's Public Works Department serves only about 8,000 customers in north Lakewood; more than twenty special sanitation districts serve the rest of the city, each with its own rules.
How do I find out which sewer district serves my Lakewood address?

The city recommends using its "My Neighborhood" address-lookup tool, or checking its printed water and sewer provider list and district boundary map, since jurisdiction depends entirely on the address.
Who is responsible for maintaining the sewer lateral in Lakewood?

Across the city and its districts, the property owner is responsible for the service line from the building to the main, including the tap connection; the City of Lakewood, Bancroft-Clover, and Northwest Lakewood Sanitation District all state this rule in similar terms.
Is pipe bursting allowed for sewer lateral repair in Lakewood?

It depends on the district. Bancroft-Clover Water and Sanitation District allows pipe bursting only with a signed waiver from the property owner, because the new pipe cannot be visually inspected the way an open-trench repair can.
Can a cured-in-place liner fix a sagging or crushed sewer lateral in a Lakewood district?

No. Lining bonds to the pipe as found rather than reshaping it, so a section that has lost its slope or been crushed out of round still needs excavation; district grade standards, such as Bancroft-Clover's 1% to 2% minimum, cannot be met by lining a sagging pipe.

Colorado Springs.metaTitle: CIPP Sewer Lining in Colorado Springs, CO
Colorado Springs.metaDescription: How Colorado Springs Utilities regulates cured-in-place pipe and sewer lateral repair, including the P.E.-stamped design rule in its Wastewater LESS 6.17 standard.
Colorado Springs.article:
A rehab standard with an engineer's signature on it

Most city sewer codes tell a contractor what pipe material is allowed and stop there. Colorado Springs Utilities goes further. Its Wastewater Line Extension and Service Standards devote a full section, 6.17, to trenchless rehabilitation, naming cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) and pipe bursting as approved methods for both mains and the private service lines feeding them. Before a liner goes in, the contractor must submit structural design calculations proving the finished liner can carry every load the trench puts on it, standing on its own regardless of the old host pipe's condition. Those numbers can't come from the installation crew. As the standard puts it, "the calculations shall be prepared under and stamped by a Registered Professional Engineer in the State of Colorado." Repair clamps are barred outright on service-line repairs, and any rubber coupling used must carry a UPC listing and get encased in six inches of concrete. It's a level of documentation most homeowners never see asked for on a lateral repair, and a fair question for any contractor bidding the job.

Who owns the sewer lateral in Colorado Springs

City code defines the wastewater service line as the pipe running from the building all the way out to, and including, its connection at the main. Section 12.5.410 puts the burden on the property owner in plain terms: keep the line in good shape, and replace any stretch that has deteriorated enough to let sewage leak out or groundwater seep in. The utility's own service-line standard echoes it, naming the tap specifically — responsibility runs "from the structure being served to the public main, including the wastewater service tap." That's worth comparing with how the water side works in the same city. Since Ordinance 25-87, Colorado Springs Utilities took over maintenance of the water line sitting in the street, out to the property line. Sewer never got that treatment — the owner is still responsible for the whole run, tap included, to the main.

Permits and who's allowed to touch the line

No repair or alteration to a service line can happen without a permit from Utilities, with a fee covering the inspection. New taps are limited to licensed master plumbers, and opening a manhole or collection line without authorization is its own violation. The utility's construction standards add more detail on top of the code: permits and payment need to be squared away at least 72 hours before a tap or connection happens, and a contractor can't backfill the trench, or let bedding obscure the inspector's line of sight, until the inspection is signed off. If a replacement crosses a property line — a shared service line reaching two houses, say — the owner has to work out a private agreement with the affected neighbor before Utilities will inspect anything.

Roots, backups, and where the utility draws the line

Colorado Springs Utilities treats root and grease backups as a private-side issue by default. Its guidance calls for professional cleaning of the four-inch lateral every two years, more often in older, tree-heavy neighborhoods where roots are constantly probing for cracks to exploit. When a blockage turns out to sit in the utility's own main, Utilities says it will help with resulting damages if its own negligence caused the stoppage, and may voluntarily put up to $12,500 toward a homeowner's cleanup even outside the formal claims process. Absent that, the assumption runs the other way — most backups start on private property, and it falls to the owner's plumber to find and fix the cause.

Where lining fits the utility's own rulebook

Because Colorado Springs Utilities wrote CIPP and pipe bursting directly into its construction standards, lining a lateral here isn't an improvised workaround — it's a named, engineered method with its own approval path. Section 6.17 describes a resin-saturated tube cured in place to form a jointless, watertight pipe running the full length of the original line, or, for a shorter localized defect, a CIPP sleeve set with camera guidance to patch just that section from the inside. Either approach still requires the same permit, the same inspection, and, for a full liner or a sliplined segment, that stamped structural design before a crew can install anything.

What a liner can't undo

None of that engineering rigor changes the physics of the material. A cured liner takes on the exact interior shape of whatever pipe it's installed inside, which means it restores strength to a cracked or corroded run but can't pull a sagging section back up to grade or round out a pipe that's been crushed oval by ground pressure. The standard's own design language requires a liner to carry its loads "independent of the existing pipeline" — an assumption that only holds if that pipeline is still roughly the shape it was built in. A bellied or out-of-round stretch has to be excavated and replaced, not lined over, and a liner can't make a four-inch lateral into a six-inch one; the utility's rules require matching the existing pipe's size on any repair.

A city built in bursts, on a lot of mid-century pipe

Colorado Springs dates to 1871, when the Colorado Springs Company platted the original townsite at the foot of Pikes Peak, and growth came in waves after that — tied to the railroad, the founding of Fort Carson in 1941, and the Air Force Academy afterward. Population grew more than 54% in the 1960s and over 93% in the 1970s alone. Census figures show about 5.3% of today's roughly 207,000 housing units predate 1940, with the pre-1960 share around 14%, and another 17.9% built between 1940 and 1969 — the era when clay and cast-iron laterals were standard. Just over 28% has gone up since 2000, mostly on PVC lines to current standards, but for the older third of the city, the engineering bar Colorado Springs Utilities has written into its rehab rules is the one a repair actually has to clear.
faq: Who owns the sewer lateral in Colorado Springs?
The property owner does, for the entire run from the building to the main, including the tap itself, under City Code Section 12.5.410 and Colorado Springs Utilities' service-line standard.
Does Colorado Springs allow cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) for sewer laterals?
Yes. Wastewater LESS Section 6.17 names CIPP and pipe bursting as approved trenchless rehabilitation methods for both mains and private service lines.
Does a CIPP liner installed in Colorado Springs need an engineer's approval?
Yes. The utility's standard requires structural design calculations for each cured-in-place liner or sliplining segment, prepared under and stamped by a Colorado-licensed Professional Engineer.
Is the water line and the sewer line treated the same way in Colorado Springs?

No. Since Ordinance 25-87, Colorado Springs Utilities maintains the water line in the street, but the sewer line in the street, including the tap, remains the owner's responsibility all the way to the main.
Can a sewer liner fix a sagging or out-of-round lateral in Colorado Springs?
No. A liner sets against the pipe it is inserted into rather than reshaping it, so a bellied section or a crushed, out-of-round pipe still requires excavation and replacement rather than lining.

Fort Collins.metaTitle: CIPP Sewer Lining in Fort Collins, CO
Fort Collins.metaDescription: Fort Collins gives lateral owners 30 days to repair a failing service line before the city can do it and bill the cost — and part of the city isn't on city sewer at all.
Fort Collins.article:
Thirty days, then the city takes over the repair and the bill

Fort Collins puts a hard number on how long a homeowner has to fix a failing lateral. Under Section 26-257(b), once the Utilities Executive Director decides a service line has deteriorated enough to let groundwater in or wastewater out, the owner gets written notice — and thirty days to complete the repair. Miss that window and the city can step in, have the work done, and add the cost to the property's utility account as a delinquent charge. It's a deadline with real teeth, and it changes the calculus for anyone weighing a quick liner job against a longer wait for bids: dragging out the decision has a cost attached that a lot of other cities never spell out.

Who's responsible for the lateral — and whether the city is even your sewer provider

City code calls the pipe a "service line" or "private sewer," defined as the run from the building to the public sewer where it joins city wastewater. Section 26-257(a) puts installation and maintenance on the property owner, who has to keep the entire line and everything upstream of it watertight and functioning. But before any of that applies, it's worth checking which utility actually serves the property. A large stretch of south Fort Collins isn't on the city system at all — it falls inside the South Fort Collins Sanitation District, a separate special district formed on July 15, 1964, that now maintains close to 250 miles of sewer line and seven lift stations across roughly 60 square miles spanning Fort Collins, Loveland, Timnath, Windsor, and unincorporated Larimer County. A homeowner inside that boundary is dealing with a different set of rules and a different call center than one a few blocks away on city sewer.

Permits and licensed contractors

No one can open, alter, or reconnect to a public or private sewer in Fort Collins without a connection permit obtained in advance, and starting the work first can draw a stop-work order plus penalties. The contractor doing any of it within the public right-of-way has to hold a separate city contractor's license under Article XI of the utilities chapter, on top of whatever county or state plumbing license they carry. The homeowner is responsible for locating the service line stub and notifying the utility when the repaired line is ready for inspection and reconnection — and any street, sidewalk, or parkway disturbed by the work has to be restored to city standards afterward.

What can't go down the lateral, and who calls a plumber for roots

Fort Collins code bars connecting roof downspouts, foundation drains, sump pumps, or any other surface or groundwater source into a sanitary sewer line — those belong in stormwater systems, not wastewater. Restaurants, laundries, and similar commercial operations are separately required to install and maintain grease interceptors when city officials determine they're needed. For an ordinary residential backup, the city's own guidance is direct: clearing roots or grease accumulation and fixing structural problems is a job for a plumber the homeowner hires, and if the clog sits between the house and the main, the cleanup costs are the homeowner's to cover, though the city will pay for janitorial cleanup of an affected basement if the blockage turns out to be in its own main line.

Where trenchless repair stands in the Fort Collins code

Fort Collins' service-line rules are largely material-and-slope rules rather than a rehabilitation manual. The city's Water and Wastewater Design Criteria Manual sets a four-inch minimum diameter for private sewer services, PVC as the only currently approved gravity pipe material, and cleanouts required at every change in alignment and at least every hundred feet. What the manual and the utilities chapter don't spell out is a CIPP- or pipe-bursting-specific standard the way some neighboring cities do — repairs still have to meet the general construction standards and pass inspection, but the code doesn't carve out separate design rules for a liner the way it does for slope or pipe size.

Where lining stops being the answer

Whatever method a contractor proposes, it still has to satisfy the same underlying rule: the finished line has to be watertight and in good working order, keeping wastewater in and groundwater out. A liner is well suited to that when the problem is a cracked, corroded, or root-intruded pipe that's otherwise still running true. It's the wrong tool when the line has lost its grade — a sagging or bellied stretch won't drain properly no matter how solid the interior surface becomes — or when the pipe has gone out-of-round from soil pressure, since a liner takes the shape of whatever it's installed inside rather than reshaping it. Either of those calls for digging up and replacing that section, and no liner increases the pipe's diameter if the existing line was already undersized for the fixtures feeding it.

An Army post that became a college town, and what's likely still underground

Fort Collins started as Camp Collins, an 1864 Army outpost built to protect the Overland mail route, and incorporated as a town in 1873. Colorado Agricultural College — now Colorado State University — was chartered in 1870, and the university has anchored the city's growth and its tech-sector expansion ever since; the population doubled in the decade after World War II. Against that history, Census figures show a comparatively young housing stock: about 4.5% of the city's roughly 73,000 units predate 1940, with the pre-1960 share around 8.9%, and 10.8% more built between 1940 and 1969. More than a third of the housing, 35.4%, has gone up since 2000. That skews the CIPP conversation here toward newer PVC laterals installed to modern standards, with the older clay and cast-iron minority concentrated in the historic Old Town core near the original fort site — exactly where that 30-day repair clock is most likely to start ticking.
faq: How long does a Fort Collins homeowner have to repair a failing sewer lateral?

Thirty days from written notification by the Utilities Executive Director, under Municipal Code Section 26-257(b). After that, the city can complete the repair and bill it as a delinquent utility charge.
Is every property in Fort Collins served by the city sewer utility?

No. Much of south Fort Collins is served by the South Fort Collins Sanitation District, a separate district formed in 1964 that maintains roughly 250 miles of sewer line, not the city's wastewater utility.
Who owns the sewer lateral in Fort Collins?
The property owner, from the structure to the public sewer main, under Municipal Code Section 26-257(a), including installation, maintenance, and repair costs.
Does Fort Collins have a specific code standard for cured-in-place pipe (CIPP)?
The city's utilities chapter and design criteria manual set general material and permit requirements for service lines but do not lay out CIPP- or pipe-bursting-specific design rules.
Can a liner fix a sagging Fort Collins sewer lateral?
No. A liner takes the shape of the existing pipe, so a bellied or out-of-round section still needs to be excavated and replaced rather than lined.

Boulder.metaTitle: CIPP Sewer Lining in Boulder, CO
Boulder.metaDescription: Boulder repaired its own flood-damaged 42-inch trunk sewer with structural CIPP lining, and its construction standards codify CIPP and pipe bursting for laterals too.
Boulder.article:
When the city's own trunk sewer needed the same repair homeowners get

Boulder's clearest sewer lining story isn't about a house at all. During the September 2013 Front Range flood, the raging South Boulder Creek tore away the ground covering a section of the city's 42-inch wastewater trunk line. As the city's own project description puts it, "During the 2013 Front Range flood, creek erosion fully exposed a portion of the line, and the creek was actively flowing over the pipe." Rather than dig up and replace the exposed half-mile stretch, the city fixed it with a fully structural, ultraviolet-light-cured CIPP liner installed inside the existing pipe, work completed as Phase 1 of the Main Sewer Improvements Project in early 2023. It's the same lining process a contractor uses on a residential lateral, scaled up to one of the largest pipes the city owns, and it's a useful data point for a homeowner wondering whether the technology holds up under real structural stress: Boulder trusted it on a 42-inch trunk line carrying a meaningful share of the city's wastewater.

Who's responsible for the lateral in Boulder

Boulder's code doesn't define "service line" in the wastewater chapter itself; that's spelled out in the city's Design and Construction Standards, which describe a wastewater service as a private extension tapped onto the collection main. Responsibility follows the same pattern as most Colorado cities: Section 11-2-19 requires the property owner to maintain the line from the city's main to the structure and keep it in good condition at the owner's expense. There's one twist specific to Boulder — the tap itself can only be cut by the city. City code reserves tap installation to "city sewer utility personnel," and the construction standards confirm that every connection tap onto an existing main is made by the city's own utilities division, paid for by the applicant. The homeowner owns the pipe once it leaves the main, but never gets to touch the actual connection point.

Permits, licensed contractors, and city-controlled taps

Installing or altering a sanitary sewer service line in Boulder requires written city permission in advance, and only a contractor licensed under the city's Contractor in the Public Right-of-Way ordinance — or someone the city manager separately authorizes — can do that work. Excavating in a public street or alley requires its own permit, and backfilling has to follow the Design and Construction Standards rather than a contractor's own judgment. A disconnection works the same way: an owner who wants to abandon a line has the city plug it at the property line rather than doing so themselves, and a new connection can't be issued until any prior service on that property has been properly capped.

What can't go into a Boulder sewer line

City code flatly prohibits connecting stormwater drains, downspouts, subsurface drainage, or boiler blow-off to the sanitary sewer system, and the construction standards list the specific offenders: roof drains, storm inlets, foundation perimeter drains, patio and parking-structure area drains, and groundwater sump systems all have to stay out of a wastewater service line. Parking garage floor drains need grease and sediment traps. That inflow-and-infiltration concern isn't abstract for Boulder — it's the stated driver behind the $70 million Main Sewer Improvements Project, since heavy rainfall events have repeatedly overloaded the collection system with water that shouldn't be getting in.

CIPP and pipe bursting, written into the standards themselves

Unlike some neighboring cities, Boulder's Design and Construction Standards carry a dedicated, detailed section for cured-in-place pipe. Section 9.19 requires the resin tube and resin system to meet ASTM F1216, requires the contractor to clear the line of roots and solids before insertion, and requires post-installation visual inspection under ASTM F1216 along with a full PACP-format camera report before and after the liner cures. Service connections have to be reopened from inside the pipe with a remote cutting device rather than by excavating down to them. Pipe bursting gets its own section too, describing a winch-driven bursting head that splits the old pipe while pulling new polyethylene pipe in behind it. Both methods sit in the standards as approved, engineered options — not exceptions a contractor has to argue for.

Where lining reaches its limit

Even with that level of standardization, CIPP has the same physical ceiling in Boulder as anywhere else. The liner sets to the interior contour of the pipe it's installed in, so it can seal cracks, corrosion, and root intrusion in an otherwise intact line, but it can't restore lost slope to a section that has settled or bellied — that still has to be dug up, because no interior coating fixes a pipe that no longer drains downhill. It likewise can't reshape a pipe that's gone oval or been crushed under soil load, and it can't turn an undersized line into a larger one; a contractor proposing to line their way past a genuine capacity problem is proposing the wrong fix.

A mining-camp founding, an aging system, and what the housing numbers say

Boulder was founded in 1858 by gold-rush prospectors and incorporated in 1871, and much of its sanitary sewer network, by the city's own account, dates back to the early 1900s — a fact the Wastewater Utility names as a continuing focus of its rehabilitation work. Census data shows why that matters at the household level: roughly 7.7% of Boulder's 46,765 housing units were built before 1940, with the pre-1960 share climbing to 18.2%, and more than a quarter of the stock, 26.8%, going up between 1940 and 1969. Only about 17.8% has been built since 2000, the smallest share of new construction among Colorado's larger cities. With that much mid-century and older housing sitting on a system the city itself describes as aging, the odds that a given lateral is original clay or cast iron are higher here than in most fast-growing Front Range suburbs — and the city's own trunk-line repair shows which rehabilitation method it's willing to bet on.
faq: Did Boulder use cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) on its own sewer system?

Yes. After the September 2013 Front Range flood exposed and damaged a section of the city's 42-inch wastewater trunk line, Boulder repaired it with a fully structural, UV-cured CIPP liner as Phase 1 of its Main Sewer Improvements Project.
Who owns the sewer lateral in Boulder?
The property owner, from the city's main to the structure, under Boulder Revised Code Section 11-2-19, though only the city can cut the actual tap into the main.
Does Boulder's code specifically address CIPP for sewer laterals?
Yes. The city's Design and Construction Standards, Section 9.19, sets material, installation, and inspection requirements for CIPP based on ASTM F1216, and Section 9.20 addresses pipe bursting.
Can a homeowner install their own sewer service line in Boulder?

No. Only a contractor licensed under Boulder's Contractor in the Public Right-of-Way ordinance, or someone separately authorized by the city manager, may install or alter a sanitary sewer service line.
Can CIPP lining fix a sagging or undersized lateral in Boulder?
No. Lining conforms to whatever shape the host pipe already has when the resin cures, so it cannot restore lost slope in a bellied section, correct an out-of-round pipe, or increase pipe diameter.

Arvada.metaTitle: Sewer Lateral Repair & Lining in Arvada, CO
Arvada.metaDescription: How Arvada, Colorado code assigns sewer lateral ownership to the city main tap, what permits and licensed contractors are required, and where CIPP lining fits.
Arvada.article:
Arvada Homeowners Own More of the Sewer Line Than They Think

Most cities describe the sewer lateral as ending at the property line or at a meter pit. Arvada's code goes a step further. Under the city's utilities ordinance, a resident's maintenance and repair obligation runs "to the tap connection, including the precast service-line wye or tapping saddle, on the city's sewer main" (Sec. 102-134). In plain terms, the fitting attached to the city's own main -- the wye or saddle that creates the tap -- is treated as the homeowner's private piping, not the city's. Few codes state this so specifically; most simply say the lateral is private up to the main. Arvada also runs a service most homeowners never expect: if a contractor runs a camera through the line, the city's Wastewater Division will watch the same video and give a free second opinion, by appointment. That combination -- extended ownership plus a free technical review -- shapes how a lateral problem here gets diagnosed and fixed.

Who Is Responsible for a Sewer Lateral in Arvada

Arvada's code defines a service line as "all pipes, fittings, and appurtenances" that move wastewater from a unit to the city sewer main (Sec. 102-32). Everything in that run -- pipe, fittings, and even the tap hardware on the main -- belongs to the property owner to maintain, protect, and repair. The city carries no liability for damage to that piping. The city's own consumer page states plainly that care of the line up to and including the connection to the main sewer falls to the homeowner. Arvada does step in for problems inside its own main: call the Wastewater Division, and city crews will check the main before pointing a homeowner toward a private plumber for anything inside the service line.

Permits, Contractors, and Street-Cut Rules

Repairing or replacing a lateral in Arvada requires a permit no matter who does the work. A homeowner may pull a permit for work entirely on private property, but anyone touching the right-of-way needs a valid Arvada contractor's license, and even private-property work needs a licensed plumber. Colorado 811 locates must be confirmed before approval. If the repair crosses into a street on the city's Street Cut Moratorium map, the contractor needs a letter to the Public Works Director and a pre-construction meeting -- a hurdle that mainly affects open-cut repairs rather than work through an existing access point. Applications take one to two business days to review, and asphalt or concrete patches carry a two-year warranty review.

Grease, Groundwater, and What Can't Go Down the Line

Arvada's code bans discharging anything but human waste and toilet tissue into the sanitary sewer, naming grease, grit, rags, and ashes specifically (Sec. 102-131); the city cites this section when warning residents about flushable wipes. Sump pumps and foundation drains are also barred from the sanitary system (Sec. 102-135), since clean groundwater eats into treatment capacity the city pays to run. Commercial kitchens need grease or grit interceptors under Arvada's adopted plumbing code (Sec. 102-136). None of these rules target lining directly, but they matter to a homeowner diagnosing recurring backups: a line clogged repeatedly by grease or roots behaves differently under a camera than one failing from a structural break, and the city's free video review can help sort that out before money is spent on a fix.

Where Cured-in-Place Lining Fits

Arvada's published ordinance does not name trenchless repair methods; detailed standards live in the city's separate engineering specifications rather than the code itself. That doesn't rule lining out -- it means the choice of repair method is left to the contractor and homeowner's judgment, within the general requirement that finished work meet city specifications. For a lateral that is structurally sound but cracked, root-intruded, or leaking at joints along a straight run, a cured-in-place liner installed through an existing cleanout is often the least disruptive option, since it avoids opening the yard, driveway, or a street that might sit inside the moratorium map.

When Lining Is Not the Right Fix

A liner sets to the interior shape of the host pipe it's placed inside -- it does not add slope, and it does not change the pipe's diameter. If a section of an Arvada lateral has settled into a belly and lost fall, wastewater will keep pooling in that low spot liner or no liner, because the finished lining just repeats the shape of the sagging pipe underneath it. The same goes for a lateral crushed out-of-round by age, tree-root pressure, or shifting soil: a liner needs a roughly round host pipe to cure against, and a badly deformed section usually has to be dug up and replaced first. A liner also can never make a pipe bigger; an undersized line stays undersized after lining. In each case, the fix is excavation of that one section, not more lining.

Arvada's Housing Stock and What It Means for Aging Laterals

Arvada's sewer network -- over 400 miles of mains carrying roughly 3.4 billion gallons a year to Metro Water Recovery's Hite plant -- has kept pace with a city that barely existed before the mid-20th century. Platted along the railroad in 1870 and incorporated in 1904, Arvada stayed a small farm town known for its celery crop into the 1940s, then grew more than sevenfold in the 1950s alone as postwar Denver suburbanization arrived, and nearly tripled again in the 1960s. Census figures put 11.5% of Arvada's roughly 51,655 housing units at pre-1960 construction, with another quarter dating to the 1940-1969 boom years -- meaning many of the city's laterals were installed during that mid-century surge, often in clay or early plastic pipe now well past its expected service life. Only about a quarter of the stock has gone up since 2000, so for many Arvada homeowners, the tap connection into the city main -- wye, saddle, and all -- is original equipment, the same age as the house above it.

Arvada's code (Sec. 102-134) makes the property owner responsible for the entire private sewer line, extending all the way to the tap connection on the city's sewer main, including the precast wye or tapping saddle used to make that tap.
Will Arvada review my sewer camera inspection for free?

Yes. If a homeowner has their service line televised, the city's Wastewater Division will review the same video and provide a free, unbiased second opinion on what it shows, by appointment through the department.
Do I need a permit to repair a sewer lateral in Arvada?
Yes. The city requires a permit for installation, repair, or disconnection of a sewer service line, whether the work is done by a licensed contractor or, on private property only, by the homeowner.
Can a homeowner repair their own sewer line in Arvada?
Arvada makes an exception allowing homeowners to perform repairs that fall entirely on private property, but a permit is still required before starting work.
Can lining fix a bellied or crushed sewer lateral in Arvada?

No. A liner cures to the existing shape of the host pipe, so it cannot restore lost slope in a sagging section or correct a pipe that has been crushed out of round; those sections need to be excavated and replaced.

Thornton.metaTitle: Sewer Lateral Repair & Lining in Thornton, CO
Thornton.metaDescription: How Thornton, Colorado code declares sewer lines owner property, why two treatment plants serve the city, and where lining fits under local permit rules.
Thornton.article:
Thornton's Code Says the Sewer Line Is Yours -- On Paper

Most cities describe lateral responsibility only in terms of a maintenance duty. Thornton's code goes further and states outright who holds title to the pipe: "Sewer service lines are the property of the owner of the property served by the sewer service line" (Sec. 74-102). That's an explicit ownership declaration, not just a repair obligation -- the city is saying the pipe between a house and the main was never city property. Thornton is also unusual in where its wastewater goes. The bulk flows to Metro Water Recovery's Northern Treatment Plant, which today serves Thornton and the Hi-Land Acres Water and Sanitation District, but the code carves out a second path: some flows are treated at neighboring Northglenn's plant under an intergovernmental agreement between the two cities, and Thornton's definitions section addresses discharges falling under "Northglenn's NPDES permit (where a discharge in the city will be treated by Northglenn POTW)."

Who Owns and Maintains a Sewer Lateral in Thornton

Thornton's code defines the sewer service line as everything lawfully installed between the main and the user's building, and states that "the responsibility of the city, including maintenance and repairs, terminates at the tap on a sewer main" (Sec. 74-87). A separate section adds the financial side: the owner pays to install the connection and is responsible for all maintenance and repair of the line (Sec. 74-101). Notably, Thornton draws the line differently for water service, where city responsibility runs all the way to the residential meter -- a contrast that surprises homeowners who assume both utilities work the same way. Combined with the ownership statement in Sec. 74-102, a Thornton homeowner is unambiguously in charge of everything from the building out to the tap.

Permits, Licensed Plumbers, and Inspection Scheduling

No one may open, tap, or disturb a Thornton sewer line without a permit from the infrastructure department (Sec. 74-221), and the work must be performed by a city-licensed plumber (Sec. 74-222); tapping the main is reserved for a licensed city contractor at the owner's expense (Sec. 74-223). A repair permit comes from either the Infrastructure Department or the Building Department, never both, and since an August 2022 change, inspections for these permits run only Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The new building sewer must then be inspected and tested under the city engineer's supervision before connecting to the public system.

Rules on Groundwater, Grease, and Basement Drainage

Thornton bars sump pumps, foundation drains, and other surface or groundwater sources from tying into a building sewer without specific department approval (Sec. 74-194), and cooling or condensate water from air conditioning is likewise kept out of the sanitary system. Businesses that generate grease -- restaurants, car washes, and service stations among them -- must install a sand or grease interceptor, and the city inspects those monthly; a failing interceptor gets two weeks to be fixed before the city does the work and bills the sewer account. Maintenance crews also routinely televise the sewer mains for root intrusion, breakage, and infiltration, which is part of why a homeowner calling about a backup is often asked whether the problem is on the city side of the tap.

Where Lining Fits in Thornton's Own Rehab Language

Thornton's construction standards do mention rehabilitating buried pipe with a liner -- but only for manholes, not for sewer service lines. New manholes downstream of a lift station have to be lined to the city's detail drawing, with previously lined manholes exempted from doing it twice. The service-line specifications themselves -- material, slope, bends, cleanouts -- are written around new pipe and open-trench replacement rather than rehabilitation technique, leaving the method of repairing an existing lateral to the licensed plumber's judgment under the general standard that finished work meet city specifications. For a lateral that's structurally intact but compromised by root intrusion or cracked joints, a cured-in-place liner run through an existing cleanout can meet that standard without the trench work the city's new-construction rules spell out.

When a Liner Won't Solve the Problem

Lining bonds to whatever contour the host pipe already has when the resin sets, and a settled, bellied section keeps its low spot afterward -- the process has no way to lift a sagging run back to grade. Thornton's own construction standards set minimum and maximum slopes for new sewer services, as tight as a 1% minimum for 6-inch pipe, underscoring how much a lateral depends on consistent grade; once a section sags below that design slope, wastewater and solids keep collecting in the low point no matter how well the liner bonded above it, and that run needs to be dug up and reset. A liner likewise can't correct a pipe gone oval or crushed by soil movement or an old root system -- it needs a reasonably intact host pipe to expand against -- and it cannot increase the diameter of an undersized line.

Thornton's Growth Boom and What It Left Underground

Thornton didn't exist as a planned community until 1953, when developer Sam Hoffman laid out what became, per Wikipedia, Adams County's first fully planned town with municipal services funded from a single tax levy; the city incorporated in 1956 with roughly 5,500 residents. What followed was extraordinarily fast growth: the population more than tripled between 1970 and 1980, from 13,326 to 42,054, and kept climbing through the 1990s and 2000s. Census figures show that pattern today -- only 5.1% of Thornton's roughly 51,088 units predate 1960, while 42.1% have been built since 2000, making its building stock among the youngest of Colorado's larger cities. That skew cuts both ways for laterals: few Thornton homes run on original mid-century clay pipe, but the volume of newer construction means most laterals are still well within their expected service life, so lining here tends to address isolated defects -- a root intrusion, a cracked joint -- rather than wholesale replacement.
faq: Who owns the sewer service line in Thornton, Colorado?

Thornton's code states directly that sewer service lines are the property of the owner of the property they serve (Sec. 74-102), and city responsibility for maintenance and repair terminates at the tap on the sewer main (Sec. 74-87).
Does all of Thornton's sewage go to the same treatment plant?

No. Most Thornton wastewater goes to Metro Water Recovery's Northern Treatment Plant, but the code recognizes that some flows are treated at neighboring Northglenn's plant under an intergovernmental sewer service agreement between the two cities.
Do I need a licensed plumber to repair a sewer lateral in Thornton?

Yes. City code requires that all work on water and sewer pipes connected to the city system be performed by a plumber licensed by the city, and a permit from the infrastructure department is required before work begins.
When can sewer repair permits be inspected in Thornton?

Since an August 2022 change, inspections for sewer and water service repair permits are scheduled only on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and the permit itself comes from either the Infrastructure Department or the Building Department, not both.
Can a liner fix a sagging or crushed sewer lateral in Thornton?

No. A cured-in-place liner sets up against whatever contour the old pipe already has, so it cannot restore lost slope in a settled section or correct a pipe crushed out of round; those sections require excavation, and lining also cannot enlarge an undersized line.

Grand Junction.metaTitle: Sewer Lateral Repair & Lining in Grand Junction, CO
Grand Junction.metaDescription: How Grand Junction's jointly owned city-county sewer system assigns lateral responsibility, bars septic in the 201 area, and where CIPP lining fits.
Grand Junction.article:
Grand Junction's Sewer System Belongs to the City and the County

Grand Junction's sewer utility isn't a purely municipal operation. Under a Joint Sewerage Service Agreement dated October 17, 1979, and a follow-up agreement from May 1, 1980, the Persigo Wastewater Treatment Plant and its pipe network are jointly owned by the City of Grand Junction and Mesa County, with the city handling day-to-day operation. The service territory, known as the "201" planning area, extends well past the city limits into unincorporated Mesa County. Inside that boundary, code adopted under an intergovernmental agreement requires all properties to connect to the system, excluding septic or other individual disposal systems, and any new development there must annex into the city rather than build out on county land. That's a structure most cities in this state don't have: a sewer utility that shares ownership and planning authority with a separate county government, and treats septic tanks as effectively off the table across a large swath of unincorporated land.

Who Is Responsible for a Lateral in Grand Junction

City code calls the pipe running from a house to the public sewer a "building sewer," defined as the extension from the building drain to the public sewer. Responsibility is unambiguous: all costs of installing and maintaining the building sewer fall on the owner (Sec. 13.04.130). The city's own utilities page puts this in consumer terms, telling residents that while Grand Junction maintains the mains, it cannot service property plumbing because that plumbing belongs to the property owner. A 2023 code amendment also updated how multiple buildings on one parcel can be served, allowing a shared service line between structures on the same lot under city-approved conditions rather than requiring a separate line for each building outright.

Permits and Standards for Sewer Work

Grand Junction requires a written permit from the City Manager before anyone connects to, opens, or disturbs the public sewer (Sec. 13.04.120), and separate permits govern work touching a public street, alley, or right-of-way, where the permittee bears full responsibility for cost and quality under the city's engineering standards. The building sewer code defers to the adopted building and plumbing codes for pipe size, slope, alignment, and materials, and every completed private sewer connection must be smooth and clear of rock, dirt, or debris along its full length before it ties into the public system. City staff retain broad inspection authority to enter properties and test compliance. Even downtown, a service line running through an alley can require its own encroachment permit -- the city council approved one such permit in early 2026 for a sanitary sewer line crossing a downtown alley.

Groundwater, Grease, and the No-Septic Rule

Grand Junction's code bars roof downspouts, exterior foundation drains, and other groundwater or surface-runoff sources from tying into a building sewer or drain that connects to the public system (Sec. 13.04.180). Commercial dischargers also face a numeric limit on fats, oils, and grease. The most consequential rule regionally is the 201-area septic exclusion above: because the city and county committed the whole planning area to sewer service, far more development around Grand Junction runs on the shared Persigo system than typical for a city this size, including parcels not yet annexed.

Where Cured-in-Place Lining Fits

Grand Junction's ordinances don't name cured-in-place lining or any other trenchless method by name; the building sewer specifications point instead to the adopted building and plumbing codes for construction requirements, leaving method selection to the licensed contractor working within those requirements. That's typical for a code written mainly around new construction and open-trench replacement. In practice, a building sewer that has aged into cracked joints, root intrusion, or minor infiltration -- but kept its shape and grade -- is a reasonable candidate for a liner installed through an existing cleanout, since the finished result still has to meet the same smoothness standard the code sets for any building sewer, without the excavation a full replacement would require.

When Lining Can't Do the Job

A cured-in-place liner takes on the exact interior profile of the host pipe once it hardens, which means it cannot correct a section that has lost its slope. If part of a Grand Junction lateral has settled and created a belly, wastewater will still collect in that low spot after lining because the cured liner simply repeats the sag beneath it -- that section has to be excavated and reset to grade. A liner also depends on a pipe that has held its original round shape; a line crushed or pushed oval by soil movement, tree roots, or age doesn't give a liner a stable surface to bond against, and usually needs to be dug up and replaced. And because a liner occupies space inside the existing pipe, it cannot correct a line that was undersized to begin with -- the finished diameter will always be a bit smaller, never larger.

An Older River City With a Boom-and-Bust Housing Timeline

Grand Junction was incorporated in 1882 at the confluence of the Colorado and Gunnison rivers, decades before most of its housing stock. Growth stayed modest until an oil shale boom in the 1970s brought new residents and construction -- a boom that ended on what locals call "Black Sunday," May 2, 1982, when Exxon pulled out of its oil shale investment in a single call to the governor. Census figures reflect both eras: 8.8% of Grand Junction's roughly 30,626 housing units predate 1940 and 19.4% predate 1960, giving the city one of the oldest housing stocks in this comparison, while another 17.9% went up during the 1940-1969 stretch. Nearly a third of the city's homes have been built since 2000, reflecting renewed growth; population grew 39.5% between 2000 and 2010 alone. For a homeowner in an older neighborhood, that history usually means a clay or older-generation plastic building sewer laid decades before the Persigo plant's 1984 opening -- pipe with a long time to develop the joint separations and root intrusion a camera inspection typically turns up.
faq: Who owns Grand Junction's sewer utility?

The Persigo Wastewater Treatment Plant and the sewer system feeding it are jointly owned by the City of Grand Junction and Mesa County under a Joint Sewerage Service Agreement dated October 17, 1979, and a follow-up agreement from May 1, 1980.
Can I use a septic system inside Grand Junction's 201 sewer area?

No. Code adopted under the city-county intergovernmental agreement requires all properties within the 201 planning area to connect to the Persigo sewer system, excluding septic tanks or other individual disposal systems, and requires new development there to annex into the city.
Who is responsible for a building sewer in Grand Junction?

Grand Junction's code places all costs of installing, connecting, and maintaining a building sewer on the property owner (Sec. 13.04.130); the city maintains the public main but does not service private plumbing.
Do I need a permit to repair a sewer lateral in Grand Junction?

Yes. A written permit from the City Manager is required before connecting to, opening, or disturbing the public sewer, and separate permits apply if the work touches a public street, alley, or right-of-way.
Can lining fix a sagging or crushed building sewer in Grand Junction?

No. Lining follows the interior surface of the pipe exactly as it finds it, so a section that has settled out of grade keeps sitting low afterward, an out-of-round crush stays out of round, and an undersized line stays the same diameter; those problems call for excavation instead.

Centennial.metaTitle: Centennial, CO Sewer Lateral Lining & Repair Guide
Centennial.metaDescription: Centennial has no city sewer utility—service comes from districts like Southgate, which requires a double permit. Learn who owns your lateral and where lining fits.
Centennial.article:
A city incorporated to stop annexation, not to run utilities

Centennial, Colorado didn't exist as a municipality until February 7, 2001, when voters approved incorporation by a 77% margin the previous September — one of the largest municipal incorporations in U.S. history at the time, folding in more than 100,000 residents from unincorporated Arapahoe County, including the former Castlewood and Southglenn areas. The push wasn't about building city services from scratch; residents wanted to head off further annexation of the area by neighboring Greenwood Village, which was expanding its own tax base. That history explains something unusual today: Centennial itself runs no sewer utility, no sewer department, and no single ordinance governing sewer laterals. Instead, service is parceled out among independent water and sanitation districts — Southgate Water & Sanitation District, the Arapahoe County Water and Wastewater Authority (ACWWA), Willows Water District, and others — each with its own boundaries and rules. The city's own residents' page puts it plainly: water and sewer service is handled by several different water and sanitation districts, and homeowners have to look up which one covers their address before they can find out who to call about a lateral problem.

Who owns the lateral depends on which district you're in

Because Centennial has no unified sewer code, lateral-ownership rules come from each district separately. Southgate Water & Sanitation District, headquartered in Centennial and spanning parts of Arapahoe and Douglas counties, defines a service line as any sewer piping upstream of the wye or saddle fitting on the district's main — everything from the district's pipe in the street back to the house. Southgate's rules make the property owner responsible for the entire service line, up to and including the connection point on the district's main, not just the pipe under the yard. ACWWA, serving other parts of Centennial, uses comparable language, defining a "stub out" as the point where a sewer lateral meets the property line — or, for an unconnected lot, a point within 100 feet of the property line for a future hookup. Willows Water District covers its own territory under a similar framework. Before discussing repair options, a Centennial homeowner has to identify their district, since that's whose rulebook governs the lateral and whose office issues the permit.

Southgate's double-permit rule: the district, then Englewood

Nowhere is Centennial's district-based system more visible than in Southgate's permitting requirement. Southgate's rules state: "No person shall cause or permit any connection to any District facility without first obtaining a Tap Permit therefor as provided in this Article 5, and obtaining a City of Englewood permit as provided in the City of Englewood Wastewater Utility Ordinance." That's two permits from two separate governments for one sewer connection — the district's tap permit, plus a wastewater permit from the City of Englewood, a city many Southgate residents otherwise have nothing to do with. The requirement exists because Southgate's flows are conveyed toward the regional treatment system Englewood jointly runs with Littleton. Homeowners doing lateral work in Southgate's territory should confirm requirements with both offices before a contractor breaks ground.

Root and runoff control lands on the property owner, too

Southgate's rules also make the property owner responsible for keeping root infiltration, storm runoff, and groundwater out of the district's system through the service line. If the district ends up doing repair work — including root-sawing in its own main — to correct a condition traced back to a failing lateral, it can bill the owner for that cost. There's no point-of-sale inspection program in the rules reviewed here, but the effect is similar: a cracked lateral can generate a bill for main maintenance its own condition caused, not just a backed-up basement.

Where a liner fits into a district-run lateral

None of Centennial's district rulebooks reviewed here name a specific rehabilitation method or pipe-material standard for laterals. What the rules make clear is that the owner carries responsibility for the line's condition and for stopping infiltration, and that repair work needs a tap permit — an Englewood permit too, in Southgate's case — before anything starts. A cured-in-place liner is usually installed through an existing cleanout, avoiding trenching across a yard or driveway, and it seals the small cracks and root-entry points that create the infiltration problem districts are focused on. For an owner whose lateral is structurally sound but leaking at the joints, lining is often the fastest way to satisfy the infiltration rule without disturbing the property.

What a liner won't fix

A liner sets against the interior wall of whatever pipe it's installed in, so it can't correct a section that has lost its fall: a bellied or sagging run holds standing water and sediment no matter how many layers of liner go inside, and that has to be dug up and reset to grade. The same is true of pipe that's been crushed or squeezed out of round; lining reinforces the shape already there rather than reshaping it. And a liner can't make an undersized line bigger — if the lateral is too small for the fixtures feeding it, a properly sized replacement is the answer, not a thinner liner down the center of it. Any Centennial homeowner should expect a camera inspection before a lining bid, since district rules put the line's condition on the owner.

Older pipe under newer development

Census figures show Centennial's housing stock skews young for the Denver metro: of roughly 42,500 housing units, only about 0.7% predate 1940 and just 3.5% predate 1960, while 15.1% were built between 1940 and 1969 and 12.4% have gone up since 2000. That tracks the city's incorporation story — most of Centennial was still farmland when districts like Southgate laid out service areas decades before the city existed. Most laterals here are plastic pipe, not the aging clay common in older Denver neighborhoods, but the 1940s-to-1960s pockets, plus original tap connections from a district's earliest build-out, remain the likeliest spots for the root intrusion Southgate's infiltration rule is written around.
faq: Does the City of Centennial run sewer service or handle repairs?

No. Centennial has no municipal sewer utility of its own. Sewer service throughout the city is provided by independent special districts such as Southgate Water & Sanitation District, ACWWA, and Willows Water District, and the city's own residents' page directs homeowners to identify their district for service and billing.
How do I find out which sanitation district serves my address in Centennial?

Check the district and utility information on the City of Centennial's residents' page, since coverage varies block by block and there is no single citywide sewer authority. Once you know your district, that district's own rules and permit office govern your lateral.
Why do some Centennial homeowners need two separate permits for lateral work?

In Southgate Water & Sanitation District, the rules require both a district tap permit and a separate City of Englewood wastewater permit before any connection is made, since Southgate's sewage is ultimately conveyed toward the regional plant Englewood co-owns.
Who is responsible for maintaining a sewer lateral in Centennial?

It depends on the district, but in Southgate's territory the property owner is responsible for the entire service line, including the tap connection into the district's main, not just the portion running under the owner's own property.
Can a cured-in-place liner fix a sagging or crushed sewer lateral?

No. A liner takes the shape of the existing pipe as it cures, so it cannot restore lost slope in a bellied section or correct a crushed or out-of-round pipe, and it cannot enlarge an undersized line. Those problems require excavation and, in some cases, full replacement.
