Littleton.metaTitle: Littleton, CO Sewer Lateral Lining & Repair Guide
Littleton.metaDescription: Littleton co-owns South Platte Renew with Englewood, treating 24 million gallons a day. See who's responsible for your lateral and when lining works.
Littleton.article:
A treatment plant Littleton doesn't own alone

Littleton's sewage doesn't flow to a Littleton-only plant. The city's municipal code defines the publicly owned treatment works serving the city as "jointly owned, in this instance, by the cities of Littleton and Englewood" — written directly into the wastewater ordinance's definitions rather than left as an informal arrangement. That plant, now branded South Platte Renew, sits along the river in Englewood and, per the plant's own materials, treats nearly 24 million gallons of wastewater a day for roughly 300,000 residents across Littleton, Englewood, and 19 other connecting communities. Littleton's stake is co-ownership, not a customer contract. That corridor has been tested before: in June 1965, a flood on the South Platte tore through the same valley, destroying 26 bridges between Littleton and the Colfax viaduct, damaging dozens of homes and trailers, and knocking out nine of the city's fifteen shallow water wells, forcing the city to run emergency water through fire hoses for months. No lives were lost in Littleton, but the flood is remembered locally as proof of how exposed South Platte corridor infrastructure can be — a history that still shapes how the jointly owned system in that valley is maintained today.

A hybrid system: direct city utility plus billed districts

Littleton's sewer setup isn't as fully delegated as some of its neighbors. The city's Department of Public Services directly operates the wastewater utility feeding the shared plant, and Title 7, Chapter 5 of the municipal code governs service lines, permits, and repairs there. At the same time, a dozen additional sanitation and metro districts inside or overlapping Littleton, among them Bow Mar, Columbine, Grant, Ken Caryl Ranch, Platte Canyon, Roxborough Park, and Southwest Metropolitan, are simply billed through the city rather than operated by it. The city's utilities page notes water and storm drainage may be billed separately from sewer, so a Littleton address alone doesn't tell you which rulebook applies.

The lateral belongs to the owner, tap and all

Where the city code applies, the responsibility rule is unambiguous. Chapter 5 defines the private sewer service line as the collector line running from a property's plumbing up to and including the connection to the sanitary sewer, then assigns maintenance of that entire stretch to the owner, including the tap to the public sewer. The owner has to keep the line in good condition, replace any section the director finds damaged, disintegrated, or prone to letting groundwater in, and complete repairs within thirty days of notice, and restore any disturbed street or right-of-way. That's a wider scope of ownership than many homeowners expect: it isn't just the run under the lawn, it's the connection point at the main itself.

Permits, inspection, and the thirty-day clock

Before service line work touching the public sewer begins, Littleton's code requires a written sewer tap permit from the city, plus a permit from any overlapping special district if one applies. Once work is done, the applicant must notify the director for inspection before the connection is buried and finalized, and the tie-in happens under the director's supervision. An existing service line can be reused for a new building only if it meets current requirements, at the user's risk; otherwise it must be plugged, with the plug inspected and approved before abandonment. Structures too low for gravity flow to the public sewer need a lift facility the owner installs and maintains at their own expense, a detail worth knowing in some of Littleton's lower-lying, older sections near the river.

What the code expects from the pipe itself

Littleton's code requires a service line's size, slope, alignment, and materials to conform to the city's separate standard specifications and the Uniform Plumbing Code, rather than spelling out a material or slope figure inside Chapter 5 itself. It doesn't name trenchless repair methods, but it doesn't rule them out either — whatever method is used just has to meet those outside standards and pass the director's inspection. That leaves room for a cured-in-place liner as a repair option, provided the finished pipe functions as required and the permit and inspection steps are followed the same as for a dig-and-replace job.

When lining isn't the right call

A liner cures against the inside wall of the pipe already in the ground, reproducing whatever shape and grade already exists — useful for sealing cracked or root-intruded sections, but no help for a run that has settled and lost slope. A bellied section still holds water and sludge after lining because the low spot in the trench, not the pipe wall, is the actual defect, and that has to be excavated and regraded. The same logic rules out lining for pipe that's been crushed or squeezed out of round, since a liner reinforces the existing cross-section rather than restoring it, and it rules out lining as a way to get a bigger pipe, since it occupies space inside the old line rather than replacing it with something larger. Given Littleton's code puts full financial responsibility on the owner within a thirty-day window, an accurate camera inspection before choosing a repair method matters more here than in a city with a longer grace period.

Housing age and what's likely in the ground

Littleton's housing stock runs noticeably older than many of its metro-area neighbors. Census data puts roughly 3.9% of the city's 21,506 housing units at pre-1940 construction and 20.2% at pre-1960, with another 26.8% built between 1940 and 1969 — close to half of Littleton's homes predate 1970, against only about 21% built since 2000. Given the thirty-day, owner-pays structure of Chapter 5, that older stock is exactly where lateral failures concentrate: original clay pipe and joints from the town's mid-century growth boom, much of it tied to postwar expansion near the Martin Marietta aerospace facilities, are old enough that root intrusion and joint separation show up regularly, and the code gives an owner very little time to sort out a repair once flagged.
faq: Who owns Littleton's sewage treatment plant?

Littleton jointly owns its wastewater treatment plant, now called South Platte Renew, with the neighboring City of Englewood. The facility treats nearly 24 million gallons of wastewater a day for about 300,000 people across Littleton, Englewood, and 19 other connecting communities.
Does the City of Littleton run all sewer service inside city limits?

Not entirely. The city directly operates a wastewater utility under Title 7, Chapter 5 of its municipal code, but a number of separate sanitation and metro districts inside or overlapping Littleton are simply billed through the city rather than operated by it.
Who is responsible for the sewer lateral connecting a Littleton home to the public main?

The property owner is responsible for maintaining the entire private sewer service line, from the structure to the public sewer, including the tap connection itself, and must complete required repairs within thirty days of notice from the city.
Do I need a permit to repair or replace a sewer lateral in Littleton?

Yes. The code requires a written sewer tap permit from the city before any service line connection work begins, plus a permit from any overlapping special district if one applies, and the connection must be inspected under the director's supervision.
Can lining fix a sewer lateral that has lost its slope?

No. A liner cures to the shape of the pipe it's installed in, so a section that has settled and lost grade will still hold standing water after lining. That kind of defect requires excavation and regrading, not a liner.

Lafayette.metaTitle: Lafayette, CO Sewer Lateral Lining & Repair Guide
Lafayette.metaDescription: Lafayette grew as a coal-mining boomtown before becoming Water Reclamation territory. Learn the tap permit, 400-foot rule, and where sewer lining fits.
Lafayette.article:
A town platted on top of a coal seam

Lafayette exists because coal was found on a farm. Mary E. Miller filed the original town plat in January 1888 and sold the first residential lot two months later, after coal was discovered on the Miller family's land in 1884 and a coal lease led to the sinking of the first Simpson Mine shaft in 1887. Mines followed quickly — the Cannon in 1888, the Spencer in 1889, and others — and the town grew into a coal boomtown: from June 1897 to May 1898 alone, more than 680,000 tons of coal shipped from Northern Field mines to Denver. Mining stayed central to the economy for decades; the last operating mine, the Black Diamond near today's U.S. 287 and Baseline Road, didn't close until 1956. That matters for sewer work today: the oldest parts of Lafayette sit directly on ground mined from underneath for close to seventy years. Coal-mining regions across Colorado's Front Range, including the area around Lafayette, are documented by the state's own geological survey as carrying a legacy of underground workings that can affect ground stability long after a mine closes — a regional, well-established pattern rather than a specific Lafayette ordinance. This pack found no Lafayette-specific rule addressing mine subsidence, so it isn't a formal city requirement, but it's worth keeping in mind when a contractor weighs excavation against a no-dig repair.

Water Reclamation, not "Sewers"

Lafayette runs its own sewer utility directly; there's no special-district patchwork here. The code chapter governing sewer service, Chapter 95, was renamed by ordinance in 2000 from "Sewers" to "Water Reclamation," a name the city has kept for its utility, bills, and treatment plant ever since. The code defines the city's treatment works as the portion of the water reclamation system owned by the city, including lines carrying effluent to the plant, sited at 750 East County Line Road. Unlike a district-by-district system, a Lafayette address has one utility and one code chapter to check.

What counts as your lateral

Lafayette's code leans on Uniform Plumbing Code-style terms rather than "service line" language. The building drain is the interior piping that collects wastewater inside a structure and carries it to a point five feet outside the building's wall. From there, what the code calls the building water reclamation conduit — also called the house connection — runs from that point out to the public conduit. That house connection is functionally the sewer lateral. The portions of Chapter 95 reviewed here don't contain a standalone sentence spelling out who bears financial responsibility for maintaining it, the way some neighboring cities' codes do; that provision may sit further into the chapter or in the building code. What the reviewed sections do make clear is that the mandatory-connection and permitting rules place the cost of connecting on the property owner, consistent with how sewer responsibility is structured elsewhere on the Front Range.

The tap permit and the 400-foot rule

Before any tap is made on a Lafayette water reclamation main, the code requires a permit: "No water reclamation tap shall be made upon any water reclamation main or any other portion of the water reclamation works of the city without first securing a permit therefor." The application states the tap size, address, and applicant's name. The code also sets a mandatory-connection trigger: if a public water reclamation line runs within 400 feet of a property line, the owner must connect at their own expense within 60 days of notice, and private disposal systems become unlawful once that threshold applies. Every water closet and plumbing fixture in city limits must tie into the public system. That same 400-foot distance appears in nearby Littleton's mandatory-connection rule, suggesting a shared model ordinance, but for a Lafayette property it's a plain, enforceable deadline.

Where a liner fits Lafayette's system

Chapter 95 doesn't name cured-in-place lining or any other rehabilitation technique, and it doesn't set a minimum slope or require a particular pipe material for a house connection. What it does establish is the permit requirement for tap work and the director's authority to review it. A liner run through an existing cleanout typically doesn't require a new tap at all, since it rehabilitates a connection that already exists. For a homeowner whose house connection is intact but cracked, root-infiltrated, or leaking at the joints, lining avoids retriggering the tap-permit process while still sealing the pipe.

What lining can't do here

A cured-in-place liner sets to the interior contour of whatever pipe it's installed in, so a section that has lost grade and sagged into a low spot keeps holding standing wastewater after lining just as it did before; the fix for a bellied run is excavation and regrading, not a thicker liner. The same holds for a connection that's been crushed, ovaled, or squeezed by shifting ground: lining reinforces the existing shape rather than correcting it, and it can't increase the diameter of an undersized line. Given Lafayette's older neighborhoods sit on ground with a documented mining history, and ground movement is a common cause of a sagging lateral in an older town, a camera inspection before choosing a repair method is worth the cost.

Older ground, newer houses

Lafayette's housing stock tells a story of two eras. Census figures show about 4.2% of the city's 13,323 housing units predate 1940 and 7.1% predate 1960 — modest shares reflecting how small the town remained through much of its coal-era history — while only 4.9% were built between 1940-1969 and a striking 31.6% have gone up since 2000, making Lafayette one of the more recently built cities in this comparison. Most Lafayette laterals are modern plastic pipe installed well after the last mine closed in 1956. But the oldest surviving houses cluster in the townsite Mary Miller platted in 1888, above the earliest mine workings, and it's those pre-1940 and pre-1960 properties where a homeowner is most likely to need a real inspection rather than a guess.

The city's Chapter 95 was renamed by ordinance in 2000 from 'Sewers' to 'Water Reclamation,' and the city has kept that name for its utility, treatment plant, and billing ever since.
Is Lafayette's sewer system run by the city or by a special district?
Lafayette runs its own water reclamation utility directly through the city's public works department. There is no special-district structure for sewer service inside city limits.
Do I need a permit to tap into or repair a sewer connection in Lafayette?
Yes. City code requires a written tap permit from the director of public works before any tap is made on a water reclamation main, stating the tap size, address, and applicant's information.
What is the 400-foot rule in Lafayette's sewer code?

If a public water reclamation line runs within 400 feet of a property line, the owner must connect to it at their own expense within 60 days of official notice, and private disposal systems become unlawful on that property once the rule applies.
Could old coal mining under Lafayette affect a sewer lateral?

Lafayette's older neighborhoods were built on ground with a documented regional history of underground coal mining active until 1956. No Lafayette-specific ordinance addresses mine subsidence for utility trenching, but the general risk of ground movement in former mining areas is a reasonable factor for a homeowner to discuss with a contractor before choosing a repair method.
